File formats

Each binary format has a specification in the repository. The paragraphs below say what each file holds.

  • Text table
  • Oracle
  • Byte-aligned list
  • Residue-class list
  • Prime wavelet tree, coded
  • Prime wavelet tree, byte-aligned
  • Path files
  • Divisor-search masks
  • Checksums and manifest

Text table

This is the source table, with one line per Carmichael number in increasing order. Each line holds n and then its prime factors in increasing order, separated by spaces, and ends in a line feed. The file has 18,358,310,309 bytes. Its authors serve it, and it is not part of the repository.

Source
blue.butler.edu/~jewebste/new_table.txt

Oracle

A lossless binary copy of the text table. It stores each n with all its prime factors, and every factor is proven prime when the file is built. Decoding it gives back the text byte for byte. Every other file is checked against it, element by element.

Specification
docs/ORACLE_FORMAT.md in the repository
Files
carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1

Byte-aligned list

A sorted list of integers (n in cell 000, dmin in cell 100). A 24-byte header is followed by VByte gaps. The first value is stored in full and each later value as its difference from the previous one, with seven data bits per byte.

Specification
docs/VBG_FORMAT.md in the repository
Cells
000, 100

Residue-class list

A sorted list of integers split into residue classes modulo M. The header gives M, which is 10,810,800 for n in cell 001 and 2310 for dmin in cell 101. Each class is stored by binary interpolative coding with centered minimal binary codes. A directory gives the position of each class, and a SHA-256 covers the header, the directory and the body.

Specification
docs/CND_FORMAT.md in the repository
Cells
001, 101

Prime wavelet tree, coded

A tree over the prime sets of one stopping divisor d per Carmichael number n. The divisor is dmin(n), d∗(n), or n itself in the trees over all primes. The most frequent primes sit nearest the root. The file is a pre-order walk of the tree. Each node stores its number of children and a terminal flag. The primes of its children are stored as gaps between frequency ranks, coded by rANS with context models. The file also holds the rank table of the primes. Decoding visits each node once and rebuilds each n from its divisor d as d times (d−1 mod λ(d)).

Specification
docs/PWT2_FORMAT.md in the repository
Cells
011, 111, 111x

Prime wavelet tree, byte-aligned

The same tree and pre-order walk with one VByte code per symbol and no entropy coding (cells 010 and 110).

Specification
docs/PWT2_FORMAT.md in the repository
Cells
010, 110

Path files

These intermediate files are rebuilt from the oracle and not hosted. Each Carmichael number has one record of 12 or 14 fields of 5 bytes. Each field holds one prime in big-endian order, and unused fields are zero. The encoders read them, and the decoders write them back in tree order. The d∗ file is rebuilt that way, from the paths it stores.

Specification
docs/PATHS_FORMAT.md in the repository

Divisor-search masks

The divisor search writes its choice in this format. An 8-byte record count is followed by one 16-bit little-endian mask per Carmichael number, in increasing order of n. Bit j of the mask selects the (j+1)-th smallest prime of n, and the selected primes form d∗(n). The masks of the published search are not hosted.

Specification
docs/MASKS_FORMAT.md in the repository

Checksums and manifest

SHA256SUMS lists the SHA-256 of every hosted file in the format read by sha256sum -c. The repository holds the same file. MANIFEST.tsv lists each hosted file with its size in bytes, bits per CN, SHA-256, cell and contents.

Ankur Gupta, Jonathan Webster and Sylvia Webster. Butler University.
